Forgotten Special Schools

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A collapse of special needs schools across KwaZulu-Natal is brewing — threatening to leave thousands of children with disabilities without classrooms, care, or support.

Unique Selling Point:
Seventy-six special schools, both public and private, all dependent on state subsidies, have either shut their doors or are on the brink of closure due to months of delayed payments and ongoing neglect by the provincial Department of Education.
The crisis cuts across every district in KZN. Truro Prevocational School in Chatsworth has already closed its gates. Ningizimu Special School in Durban is struggling to meet even its most basic needs. In uMhlathuze, Isikhwezi Special School has been forced to suspend operations amid a worsening financial meltdown, with teachers going unpaid and critical services collapsing.
Behind these names are real children — some of the province’s most vulnerable learners — now left without food, therapy, transport, or education. Many cannot access public transport safely, and for some, school meals are their only guaranteed source of nutrition.


Summary:
The situation is being described by education activists as a humanitarian emergency. What was once seen as administrative inefficiency has now spiralled into a systemic failure driven by years of underfunding, mismanagement, and indifference.
If urgent intervention does not come soon, KwaZulu-Natal could face the complete collapse of its special needs education system, effectively abandoning the very children the Constitution promises to protect.
Special schools, which cater for learners living with disabilities, are collapsing under the weight of systemic neglect. Many have been unable to pay staff, run school transport, or cover basic operational costs like electricity and insurance. In Chatsworth, the Truro Prevocational School has officially shut its doors after becoming insolvent. In Dundee, Pro Nobis School for Learners with Special Needs — home to more than 300 children — is on the brink of closure.
These are not isolated incidents. They are symptoms of a provincial crisis that has been unfolding for months.
While the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Education admits to “delays in the payment process,” its reassurances have done little to restore trust. Parents, teachers and governing bodies — led by the South African Association for Special Education (SANASE) — insist that the crisis extends beyond late subsidies. They demand systemic change: reliable transport for every school, sufficient support staff, new hostels for displaced learners, and urgent appointments of psychologists, nurses, and occupational therapists.


Further information:
The implications are severe. Thousands of learners with disabilities have now been out of school for weeks. For many, their education and therapy sessions are their only path to development and inclusion. Each day the schools stay closed, the gap widens — threatening not only the children’s futures but also the constitutional rights to basic education and equality.
The department’s repeated failures point to a deeper rot: chronic underfunding, poor management, and a disregard for the unique needs of learners with disabilities. Just months ago, similar protests saw learners and parents marching to the Premier’s office. The department promised new buses and staff posts. Those promises remain unfulfilled.
Now, SANASE and parents say they will not reopen schools until there is concrete action — not press statements.
This is a story about more than missed payments. It’s about an education system that continues to fail its most vulnerable citizens. It’s about dignity denied, rights ignored, and a generation of children left behind.
At its heart, this is the question: if the government cannot protect and educate children with special needs, what does that say about the state of education in South Africa today?

Press Release:


Forgotten And Failing
Special needs schools across KwaZulu-Natal are in crisis, with months of unpaid subsidies forcing dozens to near-collapse. Seventy-six schools that care for children with disabilities are now unable to provide food, therapy, transport, or safe learning spaces. And parents are taking a drastic step: closing down the schools they say are failing their children. This is a story about more than missed payments. Behind the statistics are real children whose rights to dignity, safety, and education are being quietly stripped away.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


Masa: KwaZulu-Natal… where some parents have made an unprecedented decision: to shut down their children’s schools.
Not out of protest… but out of desperation.
Masa: Of the more than 500 special needs schools across South Africa, 83 are located in KwaZulu-Natal.
Masa: Together, they serve over 22,000 children — learners living with autism, intellectual and developmental delays, visual and hearing impairments, and a range of physical disabilities.
Masa: Today, most of these schools are on the brink.
Parent One: That is why we've decided to close the gates, because we want answers.
Masa: Funding arrives late — or doesn’t arrive at all.
Khetha: This is the only bus working for the whole school - almost 500 kids.
Masa: Transport is broken.
Masa: Support staff are missing. And infrastructure, where it exists, is collapsing.
Dudu: We don't have a sick bay. Some of them are epileptic.
Masa: Parents have held these schools together for years — through donations, fundraising, and sacrifice.
Masa:But in October THIS year, the burden became too heavy.
And for some, those locked gates may be permanent.
Masa: Inkosi Thathezakhe is the only special needs school in the entire Nquthu area. It services around at least four villages which are vastly apart. It’s a massive area. The school currently caters to around 300 learners with an even longer waiting list so clearly there’s a huge demand.
Masa: Parents were shown plans for a proper brick-and-mortar school in 2012.
Masa: The School Governing Body chairperson Dudu Moloi says what they got was containers.
Dudu: When it’s summer, they become very very hot. Just imagine a child that is epileptic and a hot environment. They get fits time and time again.
Masa: Three hundred and twenty-two learners share just four container classrooms. The fifth? It serves as everything else.
Dudu: This is our principal's office. It’s a storeroom, it's an office, it’s a sick bay. It’s everything. It’s one office and it does everything.
Masa: There is no medical professional on site, leaving teachers to step into roles they were never trained for — a clear breach of the Department’s own Guidelines for Special Schools, which require specialist support staff, like therapists, psychologists and sign-language interpreters.
Dudu: They become nurses because there are kids that need medication, so they need to take medication at a certain time. So when there is no nurse there, how do you go about doing that?
Masa: These children have specific special needs that require medical attention, proper facilities and infrastructure. And these containers are clearly inadequate.
Masa: Special schools in KZN are supposed to receive subsidies three times a year — known as ‘tranche payments’.
Masa: But they often arrive late, or not at all. And at Pro Nobis School in Dundee, the delays have been devastating.
Masa: SGB Member Sicelo Madondo says the school is being crippled by the wait.
Sicelo: The first tranch was supposed to be paid in April 2025. It was only paid in July.
Masa: That funding was released only in October — three months late.
Sicelo: Each tranch has got 600 thousand and 99 000 is reversed for all operations. We pay like R135 000 per month, 165 000 per month to the municipality for electricity alone.
Masa: Once the utilities are paid, almost nothing is left for essentials or support staff.
Masa: The crisis stretches across the province. On the south coast, parents at Schola Amoris have also reached a breaking point.
Parent Three: The mainstream schools have received the first, second and third trenches. But we only received the first tranche. What's supposed to happen with us and our children?
Masa: This is a story about more than unpaid subsidies. It’s about an education system that continues to fail its most vulnerable citizens. It’s about dignity denied, rights ignored and a whole generation of children just left behind.
Masa: Situated between Roosboom, Ezakheni, Matiwane and Steadville - Inkanyezi Special School faces a major hurdle: transport.
Masa: With just one working bus to reach learners across these distant communities, the school can only serve one area per week, leaving others to wait.
Masa: The Deputy Chairperson of the South African National Association for Special Schools Education Khetha Khumalo says pupils are absent for weeks — sometimes an entire month.
Masa: So Baba Khumalo I hear this is your only working bus in this whole school?
Khetha: Yes, for the entire 500 kids.
Masa: And how many kids does it take?
Khetha: It's taking 47 seated.
Masa: Out of hundreds of kids?
Khetha: Yes.

Khetha: This week, we maybe you can go to Ezakheni. Then the following week is go to Peace Town, Driefontein and that side. So we are rotating the bus.
Masa: If you live in an area where the bus isn't going for that week, your kid mustn't come to school, basically?
Khetha: That's the problem. If tomorrow this bus is broken, you gonna go another six months.
Masa: And what happens to those day kids?
Khetha - Nothing. We have no plan. The kids are not are not coming to school.
Masa: When the bus doesn’t run… Phindile Mlotshwa’s 15 year old son - stays home. He has a neurological learning disability.
Phindile - He stays at home until his turn comes for the bus to collect him.
I don’t have the means or money to take him to school myself.
Masa: She does what she can to keep him learning - but there are no easy solutions.
Masa - Do you get scared when he uses public transport?
Phindile: I do get scared, because sometimes you have to call the teacher to confirm that he got into the taxi. I tell them he got into the taxi around 7 a.m. Then I'm asking, "Has he arrived yet?". As a parent you're always scared about whether he'll get to school safely.
Masa : And having her son at home means Phindile has had to quit her job to take care of him.
Phindile: I’m so hurt. Because I also need to go to work so that we have something to eat. But how do I do that when my child is here at home? How do I leave and go to work? The child is here at home - he needs my attention. We've explained to the Department that our children have different types of conditions. There are some who you can't leave unattended. This means you have to stay home as well as a parent.
Masa: From the outside, Inkanyezi looks impressive. But inside… the cracks run deep.
Masa: The geyser hasn’t worked since the school was handed over eight years ago.
Khetha: These are industrial gysers. No one else can come and fix it anyway. So we must come with a plan.
Masa: So basically, you take a big plastic bucket.
Khetha: Yes.
Masa: And you warm up the water.
Khetha: You put the element on the plastic bucket, the big one, and then we warm up with the water so that we can bath the kids.
Masa: In 2022, then-MEC Mbali Frazer promised Thathezakhe would get permanent buildings in 2023. It never happened.
Masa: Under current MEC Sipho Hlomuka… parents say nothing has changed.
Dudu: You as the head of department, Im sorry if I'm going to sound rude. If you, as a person who is responsible for making sure that they get whatever it is that they need - You say there's no money, what do you expect to happen?
Masa: While some schools eventually received overdue subsidies, others did not. SANASE requested a meeting with the KZN Education Department this week, but officials did not attend. As a result, parents have decided not to reopen schools in 2026.
Dudu: You voted this government into power, but today the same government is looking down on the rights of your own children.
Dudu: The KZN education department declined a formal interview.
But families say they will continue to fight — so that their children are not forgotten.

The child is here at home - he needs my attention. We've explained to the Department that our children have different types of conditions. There are some who you can't leave unattended. This means you have to stay home as well as a parent. Masa: From the outside, Inkanyezi looks impressive. But inside… the cracks run deep. Masa: The geyser hasn’t worked since the school was handed over eight years ago. Khetha: These are industrial gysers. No one else can come and fix it anyway. So we must come with a plan. Masa: So basically, you take a big plastic bucket. Khetha: Yes. Masa: And you warm up the water. Khetha: You put the element on the plastic bucket, the big one, and then we warm up with the water so that we can bath the kids. Masa: In 2022, then-MEC Mbali Frazer promised Thathezakhe would get permanent buildings in 2023. It never happened. Masa: Under current MEC Sipho Hlomuka… parents say nothing has changed. Dudu: You as the head of department, Im sorry if I'm going to sound rude. If you, as a person who is responsible for making sure that they get whatever it is that they need - You say there's no money, what do you expect to happen? Masa: While some schools eventually received overdue subsidies, others did not. SANASE requested a meeting with the KZN Education Department this week, but officials did not attend. As a result, parents have decided not to reopen schools in 2026. Dudu: You voted this government into power, but today the same government is looking down on the rights of your own children. Dudu: The KZN education department declined a formal interview. But families say they will continue to fight — so that their children are not forgotten.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A collapse of special needs schools across KwaZulu-Natal is brewing — threatening to leave thousands of children with disabilities without classrooms, care, or support.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Seventy-six special schools, both public and private, all dependent on state subsidies, have either shut their doors or are on the brink of closure due to months of delayed payments and ongoing neglect by the provincial Department of Education. The crisis cuts across every district in KZN. Truro Prevocational School in Chatsworth has already closed its gates. Ningizimu Special School in Durban is struggling to meet even its most basic needs. In uMhlathuze, Isikhwezi Special School has been forced to suspend operations amid a worsening financial meltdown, with teachers going unpaid and critical services collapsing. Behind these names are real children — some of the province’s most vulnerable learners — now left without food, therapy, transport, or education. Many cannot access public transport safely, and for some, school meals are their only guaranteed source of nutrition.
metadata.Summary: The situation is being described by education activists as a humanitarian emergency. What was once seen as administrative inefficiency has now spiralled into a systemic failure driven by years of underfunding, mismanagement, and indifference. If urgent intervention does not come soon, KwaZulu-Natal could face the complete collapse of its special needs education system, effectively abandoning the very children the Constitution promises to protect. Special schools, which cater for learners living with disabilities, are collapsing under the weight of systemic neglect. Many have been unable to pay staff, run school transport, or cover basic operational costs like electricity and insurance. In Chatsworth, the Truro Prevocational School has officially shut its doors after becoming insolvent. In Dundee, Pro Nobis School for Learners with Special Needs — home to more than 300 children — is on the brink of closure. These are not isolated incidents. They are symptoms of a provincial crisis that has been unfolding for months. While the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Education admits to “delays in the payment process,” its reassurances have done little to restore trust. Parents, teachers and governing bodies — led by the South African Association for Special Education (SANASE) — insist that the crisis extends beyond late subsidies. They demand systemic change: reliable transport for every school, sufficient support staff, new hostels for displaced learners, and urgent appointments of psychologists, nurses, and occupational therapists.
metadata.Further information: The implications are severe. Thousands of learners with disabilities have now been out of school for weeks. For many, their education and therapy sessions are their only path to development and inclusion. Each day the schools stay closed, the gap widens — threatening not only the children’s futures but also the constitutional rights to basic education and equality. The department’s repeated failures point to a deeper rot: chronic underfunding, poor management, and a disregard for the unique needs of learners with disabilities. Just months ago, similar protests saw learners and parents marching to the Premier’s office. The department promised new buses and staff posts. Those promises remain unfulfilled. Now, SANASE and parents say they will not reopen schools until there is concrete action — not press statements. This is a story about more than missed payments. It’s about an education system that continues to fail its most vulnerable citizens. It’s about dignity denied, rights ignored, and a generation of children left behind. At its heart, this is the question: if the government cannot protect and educate children with special needs, what does that say about the state of education in South Africa today?
